title: Land Value Tax UK: what 1.28% would actually cost you (Liam, WealthR / 'Quietly Compounding,' Edinburgh, 31 August 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full page fetched directly via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, no paywall, no bot-wall). Parsed to clean text; the complete blog post — all worked examples, framing arguments, calculator cross-sell, and disclaimers — was read in full. Full-text fetch, no partial or secondary source.
claim_grade: D — WealthR Ltd (Registered in Scotland SC900929, Edinburgh) is a commercial wealth-tracking/fintech company, explicitly 'not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority' per its own footer, publishing this piece on a content-marketing blog ('Quietly Compounding') that closes by asking readers to 'mark WealthR as a preferred source' for search visibility and pushes its own 'proportional property tax calculator' tool. Under EDITORIAL §4c this is a commercial/advocacy source — Tier 2 at best, and it originates no claim of its own (all figures are explicitly attributed to Tax Policy Associates), so it cannot even serve as a Tier-2 origin citation; it is pure re-presentation.
content_summary: The entire substantive content is a restatement of Dan Neidle/Tax Policy Associates' existing 1.28% UK LVT model (already on research/tpa-what-would-lvt-do.md), wrapped in explanatory framing: land is 'about 55% of housing value' UK-wide on average; a worked example that a £400,000 house costing £180,000 to rebuild sits on ~£220,000 of land value; and a comparison converting Fairer Share's 0.48% proportional-property-tax rate and TPA's 1.28% land-only rate onto a common property-value basis (~0.70% equivalent for the LVT). Verbatim worked examples: 'A £200,000 four-bedroom house in Blackpool — about £459 a year, against roughly £2,100 of council tax today'; 'A £520,000 flat in Islington — about £5,600 a year, against roughly £2,000 today'; 'A £3.4m house in the same part of London — about £12,800 a year.' The piece correctly and usefully notes: 'A land value tax is a proposal, not policy... The Autumn Budget is on 28 October 2026 and nothing here is confirmed,' and that only the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (mansion tax, homes >£2m, Nov 2025 Budget) has actually passed. Article's own line: 'Sources: Tax Policy Associates.'
existing_wiki_coverage: The Blackpool (£459 vs ~£2,100) and Islington (£2,000 vs ~£5,600) worked examples are already on research/tpa-what-would-lvt-do.md, sourced directly to TPA's own primary modelling — this piece contributes nothing new to those specific figures. people/andy-burnham.md already carries the 1.28%/69%/31% LVT headline and a Band D/Band H worked comparison (via Inman/Guardian and Forrest/i Paper), both closer to primary reporting than this third-hand commercial blog. The only original-ish element — expressing 0.48% PPT and 1.28% LVT on a common ~0.70%-of-property-value basis for comparison — is WealthR's own arithmetic gloss, not new fact, and is interpretive rather than citable content.
uncertainties: 1. Author given only as 'Liam, Edinburgh' with no surname or credentials anywhere on the page or site — cannot assess named-author standing. 2. WealthR's company registration is genuine but the company appears very new; no evidence anywhere on the site of independent original tax modelling capacity beyond restating others' figures. 3. Did not independently re-verify the underlying TPA figures against research/tpa-what-would-lvt-do.md's own sourcing in this session, since the wiki page's existing citation is itself already primary-sourced and this piece adds no new number to check.

content_summary: States plainly, as of September 2026: 'The split-rate proposal has not yet been formally introduced in Baltimore's council calendar, but the policy conversation has moved from concept to active discussion.' References an earlier 'Issue 6' piece, 'Baltimore's Next Move Is a Split-Rate Land Tax' (not in this queue, not fetched).
existing_wiki_coverage: This is a status-quo confirmation, not new information, of concepts/split-rate-taxation.md's existing 'Baltimore (2026)' paragraph, which already documents Councilman Zac Blanchard's July 2026 bill calling for a hearing (not an enacted split rate), the ~11,600-vacant-property backdrop, and the separate vacant/abandoned-property rate escalation (tripling 1 July 2026, quadrupling 1 July 2027, expiring 2029) — all sourced there to Baltimore Banner/CBS Baltimore/Baltimore Sun. It gives no bill number, hearing date, or proposed rate ratio beyond what the wiki already has. Also directly adjacent to, but does not engage, mass-appraisal-methods.md's coverage of Chester Harvey's Baltimore hedonic land-value model — that is a valuation-accuracy question, this is a political-status question; the two remain correctly distinct per the wiki's existing cross-link.
